name: Breuss cure

lead: The Breuss cure is a fasting protocol created by Austrian naturopath Rudolf Breuss (1899-1990). Followers take only vegetable juices, mainly red beet, carrot and celery root, plus herbal teas for 42 days. It was devised as a cancer treatment, not a beauty regimen.

In looks-oriented circles it is grouped with juice cleanses and fasts that people try to lose weight or get a lighter, clearer-looking body. Published research is limited to reviews of cancer diets, which found no clinical studies showing benefit and noted malnutrition risk.

paras: The protocol as described by Breuss involves no solid food for 42 days, with juices made from a set vegetable mix and herbal teas. People interested in it as a cleanse often adapt it into shorter juice fasts.

Reviews of popular cancer diets, including the Breuss cure, report malnutrition and side effects and found no clinical studies with positive survival results. Cancer Research UK and others warn restricted diets can cause malnutrition. Anyone with a medical condition, pregnancy or eating-disorder history is generally advised to consult a clinician before fasting.

angle.text: Followers of juice cleanses describe a lighter, leaner look from a prolonged liquid diet. For the Breuss protocol specifically, the stated purpose is cancer treatment and appearance effects are individual reports.

lead: The Breuss cure, also called the Breuss diet, is a 42-day fast on vegetable juices and herbal teas promoted by Rudolf Breuss, an Austrian naturopath (1899-1990).[1] Breuss held that cancer cells depend on protein from solid food and that abstaining would starve tumours.[1] His juice blend is roughly 55% red beet root, 20% carrot, 20% celery root, 3% raw potato and 2% radish.[1]

Outside its cancer origins, the regimen is discussed alongside juice fasts and cleanses, which people use hoping to drop weight, de-bloat and look fresher. Those appearance goals are claims made by individuals and cleanse advocates rather than outcomes documented for this protocol.

Research consists of reviews of cancer diets. A 2012 systematic review named the Breuss cure among the most discussed German cancer diets and found no clinical study reporting positive survival outcomes, with data instead showing malnutrition and side effects.[2] A 2014 review likewise found no clinical evidence supporting such diets and noted potential harm.[3]

paras: The protocol removes solid food for six weeks. The juice is made mainly of red beet root, carrot and celery root with small amounts of raw potato and radish, alongside herbal teas.[1] Breuss said more than 45,000 people had been cured, and his book reportedly sold over a million copies.[1]

Edzard Ernst has said the cure lacks scientific evidence and biological plausibility and that its restrictive diet risks malnutrition.[1] Cancer Research UK says restricted diets of this kind can cause malnutrition, and the Cancer Association of South Africa said in 2020 that the diet contains no known substances that can cure cancer, while describing a vegetable-based diet as healthy in general.[1]

No trials of the Breuss cure as a cosmetic or weight-loss regimen have been published. A 1987 Swiss journal article discussed the method as a cancer cure.[4] The 2012 systematic review of cancer diets found no clinical study showing survival benefit and reported malnutrition and side effects;[2] a 2014 review reached a similar conclusion and called for oncologists to counsel patients on such diets.[3]
